glosses: to stand, to bear, to endure, to withstand, to hold out
выдерживать
держать
выдерживать; выносить
nie poddawać się działaniu pewnych sił
trzymać kogoś przez pewien czas w jakimś położeniu
To endure without yielding; to withstand.

examples.text: The old oak tree abides the wind endlessly.

glosses: To bear patiently.

examples.text:
VVe will be Kings and Lords within our ſelues,
And not abide the pride of tyrranie.
"I never could abide shoemakers," said an old servant,—and it ended in her marrying one.
Neuer neuer: ſhe would alwayes ſay ſhee could not abide M[aster] Shallow.
We are vegetarian leaning, dislike smoking and alcohol, cannot abide drugs.
By God sir. I will not abide another toe.

glosses: To pay for; to stand the consequences of.

examples.text: Diſparage not the faith thou doſt not know, / Leſt to thy perill thou abide it deare.
If it be found ſo, ſome will deere abide it.
Ay me, they little know / How dearly I abide that boaſt ſo vaine, / Under what torments inwardly I groane[…]

glosses: Used in a phrasal verb: abide by (“to accept and act in accordance with”).

examples.text: The new teacher was strict and the students did not want to abide by his rules.

glosses: To wait in expectation.

examples.text: And Abraham ſaid vnto his yong men, Abide you here with the aſſe, and I and the lad will goe yonder and worſhip, and come againe to you.

glosses: To pause; to delay.
To stay; to continue in a place; to remain stable or fixed in some state or condition; to be left.

examples.text: One generation passeth away, and another generation commeth: but the earth abideth for euer.
Let euery man abide in the ſame calling wherein he was called.
But they constrained him, saying, Abide with vs, for it is towards euening, and the day is farre spent: And he went in, to tarrie with them.

glosses: To have one's abode.

examples.text: "As how, my lambkin," blushing, she replide, / "Because I in this dancing schoole abide? / If that it be, that breede's this discontent, / We will remoue the camp incontinent: / For shelter onelie, sweete heart, came I hither, / And to auoide the troblous stormie weather; / But now the coaste is cleare, we will be gonne, / Since, but thy self, true louer I haue none."
And her brother and her mother ſaid, Let the damſell abide with vs a few dayes, at the leaſt ten ; after that, ſhe ſhall goe.
In empty hush, in airless gloom, Mr. Knott abode, in the large room set aside for his exclusive enjoyment, and that of his attendant.

glosses: To endure; to remain; to last.

examples.text: The Dude abides.

glosses: To stand ready for; to await for someone; watch for.

examples.text: Saue that the holy Ghoſt witneſſeth in euery city, ſaying that bonds and afflictions abide me.
I will abide the coming of my lord.

glosses: To endure or undergo a hard trial or a task; to stand up under.

examples.text: […]And shalt abide her judgment on it.

glosses: To await submissively; accept without question; submit to.

examples.text: The grand Conſpirator, Abbot of Weſtminſter, / With clog of Conſcience, and ſowre Melancholly, / Hath yeelded vp his body to the graue : / But here is Carlile, liuing to abide / Thy Kingly doome, and ſentence of his pride.

glosses: To continue or carry on, despite obstacles or hardships; to persist.

examples.text: The singer's popularity endured for decades.

[…] The life that almost dies in me:
That dies not, but endures with pain,
⁠And slowly forms the firmer mind,
⁠Treasuring the look it cannot find,
The words that are not heard again.

glosses: To tolerate or put up with something unpleasant.
To last.

examples.text: Our love will endure forever.
He ſhall leane vpon his houſe, but it ſhall not ſtand: he ſhal hold it faſt, but it ſhall not endure.

glosses: To remain firm, as under trial or suffering; to suffer patiently or without yielding; to bear up under adversity; to hold out.

examples.text: Can thine heart indure, or can thine hands be ſtrong in the dayes that I ſhall deale with thee?

glosses: To suffer patiently.

examples.text: He endured years of pain.

Dirk Kuyt sandwiched a goal in between Carroll's double as City endured a night of total misery, with captain Carlos Tevez limping off early on with a hamstring strain that puts a serious question mark over his participation in Saturday's FA Cup semi-final against Manchester United at Wembley.

glosses: To indurate.
To endure, tolerate, suffer through, or allow, especially something annoying.

examples.text: I put up with a lot of nonsense, but this is too much.
Will you be able to put up with me for another 56 more years?

glosses: To be taken in; to be sheltered (put up).

examples.text: Thousands of teens in foster care would love to put up with you.
We put up with a family friend, who was an extremely gracious and hospitable host.

glosses: To rise from a lying or sitting position.

examples.text: Stand up, then sit down again.

He tried to persuade Cicely to stay away from the ball-room for a fourth dance.[…]But she said she must go back, and when they joined the crowd again[…]she found her mother standing up before the seat on which she had sat all the evening searching anxiously for her with her eyes, and her father by her side.

glosses: To bring something up and set it into a standing position; to set something up.

examples.text: Laura stood the sofa up on end.

glosses: (stand someone up) To avoid a prearranged meeting, especially a date, with (a person) without prior notification; to jilt or shirk.

examples.text:
— What?! Why did you come HERE then? You should be at a hospital!
— A gentleman never stands a lady up.
John stood Laura up at the movie theater.

glosses: To last or endure over a period of time.

examples.text: Both Venus 5 and Venus 6 had apparently stood up well under the rigors of their 217-million-mile trips.

glosses: To continue to be believable, consistent, or plausible.

examples.text: Ehrlichman's story did not stand up under Neal's grilling.
This kind of evidence wouldn't stand up in court.

glosses: To stand immediately behind the wicket so as to catch balls from a slow or spin bowler, and to attempt to stump the batsman.
To launch, propel upwards

examples.text: It was a dreadful goal to concede as Ariel Ibagaza was able to take a short corner and then receive the return ball in space on the left. He stood up a floated cross into the middle where Fuster arrived unmarked to steer a header into the corner.

glosses: To formally activate and commission (a unit, formation, etc.).
To make one's voice heard, to speak up.

examples.text: But my biblical and theological commitments tell me we need to stand up and be counted for the issues of neighbor care and creation care. We need to speak up.

We're a lion sitting under the tree, watching the hyenas as they stalk our territory. They're coming right up to us. They scratch. They push. They're eating our food! At a certain point, we need to remember that we're a f***ing lion. We need to stand up, and we need to f**ing roar!
Don't we as citizens deserve the truth? We need to stand up and demand answers.
We need to stand up and stop this happening right here right now. China needs to know the United States will not tolerate the wholesale thievery of U.S. technology and trade secrets.

glosses: To serve in a role during a wedding ceremony.

examples.text: Will you stand up for me (as my best man) at the wedding?
The bridesmaids will stand up over there during the ceremony.

glosses: To maintain, or keep in existence.

examples.text: The professor had trouble sustaining students’ interest until the end of her lectures.
The city came under sustained attack by enemy forces.
Sam managed to sustain his erection for two straight hours.

All the beliefs, habits, tastes, emotions, mental attitudes that characterize our time are really designed to sustain the mystique of the Party and prevent the true nature of present-day society from being perceived.

glosses: To provide for or nourish.

examples.text: provisions to sustain an army
Yea, forty years didst thou sustain them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing; their clothes waxed not old, and their feet swelled not.
We rode five farsakhs today, sustained by a single bowl of curds and tortured by the wooden saddles.

glosses: To encourage or sanction (something).
To experience or suffer (an injury, etc.).

examples.text: The building sustained major damage in the earthquake.

[…] if you omit
The offer of this time, I cannot promise
But that you shall sustain moe new disgraces,
With these you bear already.

Shall Turnus then such endless Toil sustain,
In fighting Fields, and conquer Towns in vain:

glosses: To confirm, prove, or corroborate; to uphold.

examples.text: to sustain a charge, an accusation, or a proposition
After the vote is taken, the Chairman states that the decision of the Chair is sustained, or reversed, as the case may be.

glosses: To allow, accept, or admit (e.g. an objection or motion) as valid.
To keep from falling; to bear; to uphold; to support.

examples.text: A foundation sustains the superstructure; an animal sustains a load; a rope sustains a weight.

glosses: To aid, comfort, or relieve; to vindicate.

examples.text: When I desir’d their leave that I might pity him, they took from me the use of mine own house, charg’d me on pain of perpetual displeasure neither to speak of him, entreat for him, nor any way sustain him.

His Sons, who seek the Tyrant to sustain,
And long for Arbitrary Lords again,

glosses: A mechanism which can be used to hold a note, as the right pedal on a piano.

examples.text: To call this music bland is to ignore the down-the-drain vocal fade-aways, the extended sax sustains […]

glosses: To resist or endure (something) successfully.

examples.text: Tests showed that a tin ceiling could withstand a temperature of 1,369° for an hour and 10 minutes, whereas plaster collapsed in 12 minutes.
Some old, underfired clay pantiles might be damaged by button mosses rooting in cracks and fissures. But most post-war tiles are hard enough to withstand a bit of moss growth.

glosses: To oppose (something) forcefully.
